items.text: Impeller Reynolds Number

| Symbol | Description | Units |
|--------|-------------|-------|
| $\rho$ | Fluid density | kg/m³ |
| $N$ | Impeller rotational speed | rev/s |
| $D$ | Impeller diameter | m |
| $\mu$ | Dynamic viscosity | Pa·s |

**Regime classification:** Re < 10 laminar; 10 < Re < 10,000 transitional; Re > 10,000 turbulent.

**Reference:** Paul, E.L., Atiemo-Obeng, V.A. & Kresta, S.M. (2004). [*Handbook of Industrial Mixing*](https://doi.org/10.1002/0471451452), Wiley, Ch. 6.
Power Number & Impeller Power

$N_p$ is the **power number**, a dimensionless constant that depends on impeller geometry and Re.

| Impeller Type | $N_p$ (turbulent) |
|---------------|-------------------|
| Rushton turbine (6-blade) | 5.0 |
| Pitched-blade turbine (45°, 4-blade) | 1.27 |
| Retreat-curve impeller | 0.3 – 0.5 |
| A310 / A320 hydrofoil | 0.3 |
| Magnetic stir bar | 0.3 – 0.5 (approx.) |

When a vessel has no measured $N_p$ the app uses a three-regime fallback for a baffled Rushton turbine: laminar ($Re \le 10$) $N_p = K_L / Re$ with $K_L \approx 70$; fully turbulent ($Re \ge 10^4$) $N_p = N_{p,turb}$; and a log–log (power-law) interpolation between the two asymptotes in the transitional regime. The interpolation approximates the measured curve, which passes through a shallow minimum near $Re \approx 10^2$–$10^3$.

**References:** Rushton, J.H., Costich, E.W. & Everett, H.J. (1950). Power characteristics of mixing impellers, Parts I & II. *Chem. Eng. Prog.* 46(8):395–404; 46(9):467–476. Bates, R.L., Fondy, P.L. & Corpstein, R.R. (1963). An examination of some geometric parameters of impeller power. *Ind. Eng. Chem. Process Des. Dev.* 2(4):310–314. Paul, E.L., Atiemo-Obeng, V.A. & Kresta, S.M. (2004). [*Handbook of Industrial Mixing*](https://doi.org/10.1002/0471451452), Wiley, Ch. 6.
Power per Unit Volume (Specific Energy Dissipation)

| Symbol | Description | Units |
|--------|-------------|-------|
| $P$ | Impeller power draw | W |
| $V$ | Liquid volume (actual fill volume, including the bottom dish) | m³ |
| $\varepsilon$ | Mean specific energy dissipation rate | W/m³ |

The mass-specific value used by all turbulence scales is $\varepsilon/\rho$ (W/kg). $V$ is the working volume entered by the user, not the flat-bottom cylinder $\pi D_T^2 H/4$ (which over-states the volume of dished vessels by ~10–35 %).

**Reference:** Paul *et al.* (2004). [*Handbook of Industrial Mixing*](https://doi.org/10.1002/0471451452), Ch. 6.
Impeller Tip Speed

Tip speed is a common scale-up criterion and relates to shear at the impeller.

**Reference:** Paul *et al.* (2004). [*Handbook of Industrial Mixing*](https://doi.org/10.1002/0471451452), Ch. 6.
Pumping Rate

$N_Q$ is the **pumping number** (flow number).  Typical values:

| Impeller | $N_Q$ |
|----------|-------|
| Rushton turbine | 0.72 |
| Pitched-blade turbine (down-pumping) | 0.79 |
| A310 hydrofoil | 0.56 |

**Reference:** Paul *et al.* (2004). [*Handbook of Industrial Mixing*](https://doi.org/10.1002/0471451452), Ch. 6.
Kolmogorov Length Scale

The smallest eddy size in turbulent flow.  Below this scale, viscous dissipation dominates.
Typical values: 10 – 100 µm in stirred tanks.

**Important:** $\varepsilon$ here is the **mass-specific** energy dissipation rate in **W/kg** (= m²/s³),
i.e. $\varepsilon = P / (\rho\,V)$, not $P/V$ in W/m³.

**Reference:** Kolmogorov, A.N. (1991). The local structure of turbulence in incompressible viscous fluid for very large Reynolds numbers. [*Proc. R. Soc. Lond. A*](https://doi.org/10.1098/rspa.1991.0075), 434, 9–13. (English translation of the 1941 *Dokl. Akad. Nauk SSSR*, 30, 301–305.)
Maximum Local Energy Dissipation Rate

The energy dissipation rate near the impeller can be 1–2 orders of magnitude
higher than the mean. Result in W/kg (m²/s³) with $N$ in rev/s and $D$ in m.

**Reference:** Grenville, R.K., Giacomelli, J.J., Brown, D.A.R. & Padron, G.A. (2017). Mixing: Impeller performance in stirred tanks. *Chemical Engineering* 124(8), 42 ([ResearchGate copy](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/319042061_Mixing_Impeller_performance_in_stirred_tanks); opens in a browser only). The magnitude of $\varepsilon_{max}/\bar\varepsilon$ is consistent with LDA measurements by Kresta, S.M. & Wood, P.E. (1993). [*Chem. Eng. Sci.*](https://doi.org/10.1016/0009-2509%2893%2980346-R) 48(10), 1761–1774.
Average Shear Rate (Camp–Stein)
Derived from equating the volume-averaged viscous dissipation to the power input:

| Symbol | Description | Units |
|--------|-------------|-------|
| $P$ | Power input | W |
| $\mu$ | Dynamic viscosity | Pa·s |
| $V$ | Liquid volume | m³ |
| $\gamma_{avg}$ | RMS average shear rate | 1/s |
**Reference:** Camp, T.R. & Stein, P.C. (1943). Velocity gradients and internal work in fluid motion. *J. Boston Soc. Civil Eng.*, 30, 219–237.
Maximum Shear Rate (Impeller Zone)

Evaluated using $\varepsilon_{max}$ from the Maximum Local Energy Dissipation Rate equation above.  This gives the peak
shear rate in the impeller discharge zone.

**Reference:** standard turbulence dissipation relation ε = ν γ̇² (e.g. Tennekes, H. & Lumley, J.L. (1972). *A First Course in Turbulence*, MIT Press, Ch. 3); $\varepsilon_{max}$ from the Maximum Local Energy Dissipation Rate section above (Grenville *et al.*, 2017).
Shear Stress

For Newtonian fluids, shear stress (Pa) is simply viscosity multiplied by
the shear rate.  Both $\tau_{avg}$ and $\tau_{max}$ are reported.

**Reference:** Paul *et al.* (2004). [*Handbook of Industrial Mixing*](https://doi.org/10.1002/0471451452), Ch. 6.
Circulation Time

| Symbol | Description | Units |
|--------|-------------|-------|
| $V$ | Liquid volume | m³ |
| $N_q$ | Pumping (flow) number | — |
| $N$ | Impeller speed | rev/s |
| $D$ | Impeller diameter | m |

The mean time for a fluid element to complete one loop through the
impeller zone. 

**Reference:** Paul *et al.* (2004). [*Handbook of Industrial Mixing*](https://doi.org/10.1002/0471451452), Ch. 9.
Impeller Torque

| Symbol | Description | Units |
|--------|-------------|-------|
| $P$ | Impeller power draw | W |
| $N$ | Impeller speed | rev/s |
| $\Lambda$ | Torque | N·m |

**Torque per unit volume** $\frac{\Lambda}{V}$ provides a scale-independent measure
of mechanical stress on the fluid.

**Reference:** Paul *et al.* (2004). [*Handbook of Industrial Mixing*](https://doi.org/10.1002/0471451452), Ch. 6.
Energy Dissipation Circulation Function (EDCF)

| Symbol | Description | Units |
|--------|-------------|-------|
| $\varepsilon_{max}$ | Maximum local energy dissipation rate | W/kg |
| $t_c$ | Circulation time | s |
| EDCF | Mixing intensity × exposure frequency | W/kg/s |

EDCF combines the **intensity** of the impeller discharge zone with the
**frequency** at which fluid passes through it. Mixing Lab uses $\varepsilon_{max}$ as the intensity term; the original definition (Smith 1985; Jüsten *et al.* 1996) uses $P/(k D^3)$, with $k$ a geometric constant, so absolute values are not directly comparable with the literature.

**References:** Jüsten, P., Paul, G.C., Nienow, A.W. & Thomas, C.R. (1996). Dependence of mycelial morphology on impeller type and agitation intensity. [*Biotechnol. Bioeng.*](https://doi.org/10.1002/%28SICI%291097-0290%2819961220%2952:6%3C672::AID-BIT5%3E3.0.CO;2-L) 52(6), 672–684. Circulation time: Nienow, A.W. (1997). On impeller circulation and mixing effectiveness in the turbulent flow regime. [*Chem. Eng. Sci.*](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0009-2509%2897%2900072-9), 52(15), 2557–2565.
Froude Number

| Symbol | Description | Units |
|--------|-------------|-------|
| $N$ | Impeller speed | rev/s |
| $D$ | Impeller diameter | m |
| $g$ | Gravitational acceleration | m/s² |

Ratio of inertial to gravitational forces.  Important for predicting
free-surface vortex formation in unbaffled or partially baffled vessels.

**Reference:** Paul *et al.* (2004). [*Handbook of Industrial Mixing*](https://doi.org/10.1002/0471451452), Ch. 6.
Liquid Height from Fill Volume (Vessel Geometry)

items.latex: H = \begin{cases} h_{dish}\,\dfrac{V}{V_{dish}} & V \le V_{dish} \\[4pt] \min\!\left(h_{dish} + \dfrac{V - V_{dish}}{\pi D_T^2/4},\; H_{max}\right) & V > V_{dish} \end{cases}

items.text:
| Bottom head | $h_{dish}$ | $V_{dish}$ |
|-------------|------------|------------|
| Flat | 0 | 0 |
| 2:1 semi-ellipsoidal (default) | $D_T/4$ | $\pi D_T^3/24$ |
| Torispherical (Klöpper, DIN 28011) | $0.1935\,D_T$ | $0.0990\,D_T^3$ |
| Hemispherical | $D_T/2$ | $\pi D_T^3/12$ |
| Shallow dished (spherical cap) | $0.1\,D_T$ | $\pi h (3R^2 + h^2)/6$ |
| Conical (half-angle θ, default 45°) | $R\tan\theta$ | $\pi D_T^2 h/12$ |
| Any curved head with measured depth $h$ | $h$ | $\pi D_T^2 h/6$ (half-ellipsoid) |

The liquid height drives the blend time, wetted jacket area and free-surface area. The partial-dish branch is a linear approximation (exact only for a cylinder). The Klöpper constants come from integrating the head profile (crown radius $D$, knuckle radius $0.1D$); values used before the 2026 review (0.0847 $D^3$) under-stated the volume by 14 %.

**Reference:** DIN 28011 (torispherical heads) and DIN 28013 (semi-ellipsoidal heads); Perry & Green (2019). [*Perry's Chemical Engineers' Handbook*](https://openlibrary.org/isbn/0071834087), 9th ed., Sec. 10 (vessel volumes).
Macro-Blend Time (95 %)

This represents the time to achieve 95 % uniformity on the bulk (macro) scale. Equivalent to $N\theta_{95} = 5.2\,Po^{-1/3}(T/D)^2(H/T)^{1/2}$. $T$ = tank diameter, $H$ = liquid height (m), $N$ in rev/s. Valid for fully turbulent flow ($Re > 10^4$) and $H/T \approx 1$; outside that range treat the value as indicative.

**Reference**: Grenville, R.K. (1992). *Blending of viscous Newtonian and pseudo-plastic fluids*, PhD thesis, Cranfield; summarised in [*Handbook of Industrial Mixing*](https://doi.org/10.1002/0471451452), Ch. 9.
Engulfment Micromixing Time

Baldyga & Bourne engulfment model – characterises the time for mixing at the
smallest (molecular) scales.

| Symbol | Description | Units |
|--------|-------------|-------|
| $\nu$ | Kinematic viscosity ($\mu / \rho$) | m²/s |
| $\varepsilon$ | Mass-specific energy dissipation rate $P/(\rho V)$ | W/kg (= m²/s³) |

**Reference:** Baldyga, J. & Bourne, J.R. (1999). [*Turbulent Mixing and Chemical Reactions*](https://openlibrary.org/isbn/0471981710), Wiley.
Damköhler Numbers
Macro Damköhler Number
Micro Damköhler Number

| $Da$ range | Interpretation |
|-----------|----------------|
| $Da \ll 0.01$ | Reaction-limited – insensitive to mixing |
| $0.01 < Da < 0.1$ | Likely insensitive |
| $0.1 < Da < 1$ | Potentially sensitive |
| $1 < Da < 10$ | Mixing-sensitive |
| $Da \gg 10$ | Strongly mixing-limited |

These bands are engineering screening thresholds (order-of-magnitude), not values from a single correlation.

**Reference:** Paul, E.L., Atiemo-Obeng, V.A. & Kresta, S.M. (2004). [*Handbook of Industrial Mixing*](https://doi.org/10.1002/0471451452), Wiley, Ch. 13.
Gas-Liquid Damköhler Number

Compares the characteristic **gas-liquid mass-transfer time** $\;(1/k_L a)\;$ to
the reaction time.

| $Da_{GL}$ range | Interpretation |
|----------------|----------------|
| $Da_{GL} \ll 0.01$ | Mass transfer is fast — reaction-limited |
| $0.01 < Da_{GL} < 0.1$ | Likely insensitive to G-L transfer |
| $0.1 < Da_{GL} < 1$ | Potentially transfer-limited |
| $1 < Da_{GL} < 10$ | Transfer-limited |
| $Da_{GL} \gg 10$ | Strongly transfer-limited |

When $k_L a = 0$ (no gas phase present), $Da_{GL}$ is set to zero (not applicable).

**Reference:** Paul *et al.* (2004). [*Handbook of Industrial Mixing*](https://doi.org/10.1002/0471451452), Ch. 13.
Solid-Liquid Damköhler Number

Compares the characteristic **solid-liquid mass-transfer time** $\;(1/k_L a_{SL})\;$
to the reaction time, where $k_L a_{SL}$ is the volumetric solid-liquid
mass-transfer coefficient:

$$k_L a_{SL} = k_{SL} \cdot a_s, \quad a_s = \frac{6\,\phi_s}{d_p}$$

The Ranz-Marshall correlation is evaluated with the particle Reynolds number based on the
**terminal settling velocity** $v_t$ (Harriott's slip-velocity approach; a conservative lower bound because turbulence raises the slip velocity):

$$Re_p = \frac{\rho_L\, v_t\, d_p}{\mu}$$

| $Da_{SL}$ range | Interpretation |
|----------------|----------------|
| $Da_{SL} \ll 0.01$ | Mass transfer is fast — reaction-limited |
| $0.01 < Da_{SL} < 0.1$ | Likely insensitive to S-L transfer |
| $0.1 < Da_{SL} < 1$ | Potentially transfer-limited |
| $1 < Da_{SL} < 10$ | Transfer-limited |
| $Da_{SL} \gg 10$ | Strongly transfer-limited |

When $k_L a_{SL} = 0$ (no solid phase present), $Da_{SL}$ is set to zero.

| Symbol | Description | Units |
|--------|-------------|-------|
| $k_{SL}$ | Solid-liquid mass-transfer coefficient | m/s |
| $a_s$ | Specific particle surface area | 1/m |
| $\phi_s$ | Volumetric solids fraction | — |
| $d_p$ | Particle diameter | m |
| $v_t$ | Terminal settling velocity | m/s |
| $\varepsilon$ | Specific energy dissipation rate | W/kg |
| $t_{rxn}$ | Characteristic reaction time | s |

**Reference:** Paul *et al.* (2004). [*Handbook of Industrial Mixing*](https://doi.org/10.1002/0471451452), Ch. 13; Ranz, W.E. & Marshall, W.R. (1952). *Chem. Eng. Prog.*, 48, 141–146; Harriott, P. (1962). Mass transfer to particles: Part I. Suspended in agitated tanks. [*AIChE J.*](https://doi.org/10.1002/aic.690080122) 8(1), 93–101.
Characteristic Reaction Time
First-order or pseudo-first-order
Second-order
Zero-order

The characteristic reaction time is taken as the **reaction time constant**
(the e-folding time, i.e. the time for the limiting reagent to fall to $1/e$ of
its initial value), consistent with the Damköhler-number definition
$Da = t_{mix} / t_{rxn}$.  Note this is **not** the 50 % half-life
$t_{1/2} = \ln 2 / k$, which is ~30 % shorter for a first-order reaction. For second order the initial-rate time $1/(kC_0)$ assumes equimolar reagents; for zero order $C_0/k$ is the time to full conversion. A directly specified $t_{rxn}$ (reaction database or user input) overrides these. The 90 %-conversion time ($2.303/k$, $9/(kC_0)$, $0.9C_0/k$) is shown for information only — it is longer and therefore not conservative for $Da$.

| Symbol | Description | Units |
|--------|-------------|-------|
| $k$ | Rate constant | mol/(L·s) (0th), 1/s (1st) or L/(mol·s) (2nd) |
| $C_0$ | Initial concentration | mol/L |

**Reference:** Levenspiel, O. (1999). [*Chemical Reaction Engineering*](https://openlibrary.org/isbn/9780471254249), 3rd ed. Wiley, Ch. 3.
Local Micromixing Time (Impeller Zone)

Same Baldyga & Bourne engulfment model, but evaluated using the **local maximum**
energy dissipation rate $\varepsilon_{max}$ near the impeller.  Relevant when
reagents are **fed directly into the impeller discharge zone**.

**Reference:** Baldyga, J. & Bourne, J.R. (1999). [*Turbulent Mixing and Chemical Reactions*](https://openlibrary.org/isbn/0471981710), Wiley.
Mesomixing Time Scales

Mesomixing acts at the scale of the feed plume / feed-pipe diameter and has
**two** characteristic time scales (Baldyga & Bourne, 1999; Myerson 2019, Table 8.1).
Mixing Lab implements the inertial-convective (disintegration) scale below.
Inertial-Convective Disintegration

Break-up of the feed plume by inertial-convective disintegration of the large
eddies. $\Lambda_C$ is the integral scale of the velocity fluctuations, set by
the feed-pipe / plume size. **Mixing Lab implements this scale** using the
feed-pipe diameter $d_{\text{feed}}$ as the length scale with $A = 1.2$:

| Symbol | Description | Units |
|--------|-------------|-------|
| $\Lambda_C$ | Integral scale of velocity fluctuations | m |
| $d_{\text{feed}}$ | Feed-pipe internal diameter | m |
| $\varepsilon$ | Local energy dissipation at the feed point | W/kg (= m²/s³) |

$A$ ≈ 1–2 in the literature; 1.2 is used here. The mesomixing Damköhler number is $Da_{meso} = t_{meso}/t_{rxn}$.

**References:** Bałdyga, J., Bourne, J.R. & Hearn, S.J. (1997). Interaction between chemical reactions and mixing on various scales. [*Chem. Eng. Sci.*](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0009-2509%2896%2900430-7) 52(4), 457–466; Bałdyga & Bourne (1999). [*Turbulent Mixing and Chemical Reactions*](https://openlibrary.org/isbn/0471981710), Wiley.
Feed-Point Energy Dissipation

The local $\varepsilon$ used for $t_{meso}$ depends on the selected feed location (Vessel Assessment / Comparison):

| Feed location | $\varepsilon_{feed}$ (W/kg) |
|---------------|---------------------------|
| Bulk (default) | $\bar\varepsilon = P/(\rho V)$ |
| Near impeller | $\varepsilon_{max}$ (Grenville *et al.* 2017) |
| Liquid surface | $0.2\,\bar\varepsilon$ |

The surface factor is an engineering heuristic; measured $\varepsilon/\bar\varepsilon$ near the surface ranges from ~0.1 to 0.5 depending on impeller type and fill (Kresta & Wood, 1993). The Bourne Protocol Test 3 uses user-defined ratios $\varepsilon_{loc} = r\,\bar\varepsilon$ for each feed location and reports $t_E$ at each.
kLa – Volumetric Mass-Transfer Coefficient (Gas-Liquid)

Van 't Riet (1979) correlation for aerated stirred tanks.

| System | $C_1$ | $C_2$ | $C_3$ |
|--------|-------|-------|-------|
| Coalescing (pure liquids) | 0.026 | 0.4 | 0.5 |
| Non-coalescing (electrolytes) | 0.002 | 0.7 | 0.2 |

| Symbol | Description | Units |
|--------|-------------|-------|
| $P/V$ | Specific power input (the app uses the **ungassed** value, which over-estimates $k_La$ when gassing reduces power by 30–60 %) | W/m³ |
| $v_s$ | Superficial gas velocity | m/s |
| $k_L a$ | Volumetric mass-transfer coefficient | 1/s |

**Note:** $v_s = 0$ (no sparging) → $k_L a = 0$. Stated validity: $V$ 0.002–4.4 m³ and $P/V$ 500–10,000 W/m³ (coalescing); expected accuracy ±20–40 %. Lab vessels below 500 W/m³ are an extrapolation.

**Reference:** van 't Riet, K. (1979). Review of measuring methods and results in non-viscous gas-liquid mass transfer in stirred vessels. [*Ind. Eng. Chem. Process Des. Dev.*](https://doi.org/10.1021/i260071a001), 18(3), 357–364.
kLa – Free-Surface (Headspace) Mass Transfer

Lamont & Scott (1970) small-eddy surface-renewal model.

| Symbol | Description | Units |
|--------|-------------|-------|
| $D_{mol}$ | Molecular diffusivity of dissolved gas | m²/s |
| $\varepsilon$ | Mean specific energy dissipation rate | W/kg (= m²/s³) |
| $\nu$ | Kinematic viscosity | m²/s |
| $D_T$ | Tank inside diameter | m |
| $V$ | Liquid volume | m³ |
| $a_{\text{surface}}$ | Specific interfacial area (free surface) | 1/m |

**Typical $D_{mol}$ values for common gases in water at 25 °C:**

| Gas | $D_{mol}$ (m²/s) |
|-----|------------------|
| O₂  | 2.1 × 10⁻⁹ |
| CO₂ | 1.9 × 10⁻⁹ |
| N₂  | 1.9 × 10⁻⁹ |
| H₂  | 4.5 × 10⁻⁹ |

**Reference:** Lamont, J.C. & Scott, D.S. (1970). An eddy cell model of mass transfer into the surface of a turbulent liquid. [*AIChE J.*](https://doi.org/10.1002/aic.690160403), 16(4), 513–519.
Miscibility Screening

**Two-tier approach:**

**1. Known-pair lookup** — Experimental miscibility data from standard references
(Perry's, CRC Handbook, Merck Index).

**2. Hansen Solubility Parameters (fallback):**

| $R_a$ (MPa$^{0.5}$) | Interpretation |
|----------------------|----------------|
| < 15 | Likely **miscible** |
| 15 – 25 | Partially miscible / borderline |
| > 25 | Likely **immiscible** |

The 15 / 25 MPa$^{0.5}$ cut-offs are screening heuristics (they are not interaction radii $R_0$ of specific solutes); always confirm with known-pair data or a test.

**Reference:** Hansen, C.M. (2007). [*Hansen Solubility Parameters: A User's Handbook*](https://doi.org/10.1201/9781420006834), 2nd ed. CRC Press.
Liquid–Liquid Dispersion Screen (Fluid Database)

| Symbol | Description | Units |
|--------|-------------|-------|
| $\rho_c$ | Continuous-phase density | kg/m³ |
| $\sigma_{LL}$ | Liquid–liquid interfacial tension | N/m |
| $\phi_d$ | Dispersed-phase volume fraction (capped at 0.95) | — |
| $d_{32}$ | Sauter mean drop diameter | m |
| $v_{drop}$ | Drop settling velocity (Stokes / Schiller–Naumann, as for particles) | m/s |
| $t_{sep}$ | Time for a $d_{32}$ drop to cross the tank diameter | s |
| $N_{min}$ | Minimum speed to keep the phases dispersed | rev/s |

Separation bands: < 1 min rapid, 1–10 min moderate, 10–60 min slow, > 1 h very stable (heuristic). $N_{min}$ is a critical-Weber heuristic with a linear holdup correction — **not** a published correlation (e.g. Skelland & Seksaria); treat as indicative. The $(1 + 3\phi_d)$ holdup term is the usual coalescence correction for low holdup ($\phi_d \lesssim 0.2$).

**References:** Chen, H.T. & Middleman, S. (1967). Drop size distribution in agitated liquid-liquid systems. [*AIChE J.*](https://doi.org/10.1002/aic.690130529) 13(5), 989–995; Calabrese, R.V., Chang, T.P.K. & Dang, P.T. (1986). Drop breakup in turbulent stirred-tank contactors. Part I. [*AIChE J.*](https://doi.org/10.1002/aic.690320416) 32(4), 657–666.
Reaction Rate (Molar)
First-order or pseudo-first-order
Second-order or pseudo-second-order
Zero-order

| Symbol | Description | Units |
|--------|-------------|-------|
| $k$ | Rate constant | 1/s (1st) or L/(mol·s) (2nd) |
| $C_0$ | Initial concentration | mol/L |
| $V_L$ | Liquid volume | L |

The rate is evaluated at the **initial** concentration (worst case for heat release).

**Reference:** Levenspiel, O. (1999). [*Chemical Reaction Engineering*](https://openlibrary.org/isbn/9780471254249), 3rd ed. Wiley.
Heat Generation Rate

| Symbol | Description | Units |
|--------|-------------|-------|
| $\Delta H_{rxn}$ | Enthalpy of reaction (negative = exothermic) | kJ/mol |
| $r_{\text{total}}$ | Total molar reaction rate | mol/s |
| $Q_{\text{gen}}$ | Rate of heat release (positive = exothermic; negative = heat absorbed by an endothermic reaction) | W |

Before the 2026 review the magnitude $\lvert\Delta H\rvert$ was used, which reported endothermic reactions as heat generation.

**Reference:** Levenspiel (1999), Ch. 9.
Feed Sensible Heat and Net Heat Load

A feed warmer than the batch adds heat that the jacket must remove; a colder feed provides cooling. Feed $\rho_f$ and $C_{p,f}$ are evaluated at the feed temperature. $Q_{\text{load}}$ is the numerator of the heat-balance ratio below.

| Symbol | Description | Units |
|--------|-------------|-------|
| $\dot{V}_f$ | Feed rate | m³/s (entered as mL/min) |
| $\rho_f, C_{p,f}$ | Feed density and heat capacity | kg/m³, J/(kg·K) |
| $T_{\text{feed}}, T_{\text{process}}$ | Feed and batch temperatures | °C |

**Reference:** steady-flow energy balance, Incropera *et al.* (2007). [*Fundamentals of Heat and Mass Transfer*](https://openlibrary.org/isbn/0471457280), Ch. 1.
Adiabatic Temperature Rise

The temperature the batch would reach if **all** reaction heat were retained
(no cooling).  Unlike the molar enthalpy alone, $\Delta T_{ad}$ accounts for
reagent concentration and the thermal mass of the mixture, and is the basis of
the Stoessel criticality classification used to rank thermal-runaway risk.

| Symbol | Description | Units |
|--------|-------------|-------|
| $\Delta H_{rxn}$ | Enthalpy of reaction | J/mol (or kJ/mol × 1000) |
| $C_0$ | Limiting-reagent concentration | mol/m³ (= mol/L × 1000) |
| $\rho \, C_p$ | Volumetric heat capacity of the mixture | J/(m³·K) |
| $\Delta T_{ad}$ | Adiabatic temperature rise | K |

**Indicative severity bands:** $\Delta T_{ad}$ < 20 K low · 20–50 K moderate ·
50–200 K high · > 200 K very high (assess MTSR and secondary decomposition).

**Reference:** Stoessel, F. (2020). [*Thermal Safety of Chemical Processes: Risk Assessment and Process Design*](https://doi.org/10.1002/9783527696918), 2nd ed. Wiley-VCH, Ch. 2–3.
Heat Removal Capacity (Jacket)

| Symbol | Description | Units |
|--------|-------------|-------|
| $U$ | Overall heat-transfer coefficient | W/(m²·K) |
| $A$ | Heat-transfer area (jacket + bottom) | m² |
| $\Delta T$ | $T_{\text{process}} - T_{\text{coolant}}$ (signed: a coolant warmer than the batch gives no cooling) | °C or K |
| $Q_{\text{cool}}$ | Maximum steady-state heat removal | W |

Q_{\text{rxn}} = -\Delta H \cdot 1000 \cdot \frac{dn}{dt}, \qquad T_{ad} = \frac{C(0)\,T_0 + \dot{m}_f C_{p,f}\, t_{end}\, T_f - \Delta H \cdot 1000 \cdot n_0}{C(t_{end})}

items.text:
Two scenarios: **batch** (both reagents charged at $C_0$, run to 99 % conversion, capped at 24 h) and **dosed** (reagent A charged; the stoichiometric co-reagent B, $n_0 = C_0 V_0$, fed at a constant rate over the dosing time, so unreacted B can accumulate). $UA(t)$ follows the wetted jacket area as the volume grows. The rate uses the fixed rate constant (no Arrhenius temperature dependence) and is integrated semi-implicitly (first order: $dn = n_B - n_B/(1 + k\,\Delta t)$; second order: $dn = n_B - n_B/(1 + k\,n_A/V\,\Delta t)$; zero order: $dn = \min(kV\Delta t, n_A, n_B)$).

| Symbol | Description | Units |
|--------|-------------|-------|
| $C(t)$ | Heat capacity of the batch (initial charge + fed mass) | J/K |
| $\dot{m}_f, C_{p,f}, T_f$ | Feed mass rate, heat capacity, temperature | kg/s, J/(kg·K), °C |
| $n$ | Moles reacted | mol |
| $\Delta H$ | Reaction enthalpy (negative = exothermic) | kJ/mol |

Terminal Settling Velocity

**Stokes regime** ($Re_p < 0.1$): valid for small or slow-settling particles.
$\phi$ is the sphericity (shape factor, 0–1).

For intermediate Reynolds numbers ($0.1 < Re_p \lesssim 800$, the validity range of the correlation) the
**Schiller-Naumann** drag correction is applied iteratively (no Newton-regime branch, so values for very large/dense particles are approximate):

| Symbol | Description | Units |
|--------|-------------|-------|
| $d_p$ | Particle diameter (typically D50) | m |
| $g$ | Gravitational acceleration | m/s² |
| $\Delta\rho$ | $\lvert\rho_p - \rho_L\rvert$ | kg/m³ |
| $\mu$ | Dynamic viscosity | Pa·s |
| $\phi$ | Sphericity / shape factor | – |

Multiplying the velocity by $\phi$ is a simple empirical shape correction (Haider–Levenspiel-type drag correlations are more rigorous).

**Reference:** Clift, R., Grace, J.R. & Weber, M.E. (1978). [*Bubbles, Drops, and Particles*](https://openlibrary.org/isbn/9780121769505), Academic Press; Schiller, L. & Naumann, A. (1935). *Z. Ver. Dtsch. Ing.*, 77, 318–320.

**Reference:** Yaws' Handbook; Perry's (2019); CRC Handbook; DIPPR correlations.

Liquid Blend Mixing Rules (Fluid Database)

$w_i$ = mass fraction, $\varphi_i$ = volume fraction (ideal mixing, no excess volume). The density rule is exact for ideal mixing; $C_p$ mass-weighting is the standard ideal-solution estimate. The viscosity rule is the Arrhenius (Grunberg–Nissan with zero interaction) form applied with **mass** fractions (the classical form uses mole fractions); strongly non-ideal blends (e.g. water/alcohol, whose viscosity passes through a maximum) can be in error by a factor of 2 or more. Surface tension and conductivity are simple volume-weighted averages (mixture surface tension is usually below the linear value). Treat blend properties as estimates.

**Reference:** Poling, B.E., Prausnitz, J.M. & O'Connell, J.P. (2001). *The Properties of Gases and Liquids*, 5th ed., McGraw-Hill, Ch. 9–10; Perry & Green (2019). [*Perry's Chemical Engineers' Handbook*](https://openlibrary.org/isbn/0071834087), Sec. 2.

Scale-Up Matching (Vessel Comparison)

The selected parameter (P/V, tip speed, $t_E$, blend time, …) is evaluated in the basis vessel at its RPM and volume. For each target vessel the RPM (at fixed volume) or the volume (at fixed RPM) is found numerically so that the parameter equals the basis value, using the full hydrodynamic model above; the result is flagged *Not achievable* when it falls outside the vessel's RPM / volume window. For P/V at fixed volume this is equivalent to $N_2 = N_1 \left(\frac{N_{p,1}}{N_{p,2}}\frac{D_1^5 V_2}{D_2^5 V_1}\right)^{1/3}$; constant tip speed gives $N_2 = N_1 D_1/D_2$.

**Reference:** Paul *et al.* (2004). [*Handbook of Industrial Mixing*](https://doi.org/10.1002/0471451452), Ch. 6 and Ch. 9 (scale-up rules).
Bourne Protocol Planning

items.latex: N = \left( \frac{(P/m)\, V}{N_p\, D^5} \right)^{1/3} \qquad \frac{P}{m} = \frac{N_p \rho N^3 D^5}{\rho V}

items.text:
Test 1 runs the reaction at 0.1×, 1× and 10× the centre specific power $P/m$ (W/kg), a 100-fold span (≈ 4.6× in $N$, since $P/m \propto N^3$); set-points outside the vessel RPM range are clamped and the achieved span is reported. $V$ is the actual working volume (m³). Test 3 feed locations use $\varepsilon_{loc} = r\,\bar\varepsilon$ with user-entered ratios $r$, and $t_E = 17.3(\nu/\varepsilon_{loc})^{1/2}$. A KPI is flagged sensitive when its largest change from the centre value exceeds the threshold (default 5 %).

**Reference:** Bourne, J.R. (2003). Mixing and the selectivity of chemical reactions. [*Org. Process Res. Dev.*](https://doi.org/10.1021/op020074q) 7(4), 471–508; Bałdyga & Bourne (1999). [*Turbulent Mixing and Chemical Reactions*](https://openlibrary.org/isbn/0471981710).

For condensing steam, the jacket-side coefficient is very high
($h_o \approx$ 6 000 – 12 000 W/(m²·K)) and is treated as a fixed value
rather than computed from a Nusselt correlation.

**Default:** $h_o$ = 8 000 W/(m²·K) for condensing steam.
Impeller Power (Agitator Heat Input)

All mechanical energy dissipated by the impeller is ultimately converted to
heat in the fluid. This is added as a heat source in the transient energy balance.

Steady-State Heat Duty

The maximum instantaneous heat removal/addition rate at any point in time.
As the batch temperature approaches the jacket temperature, $\Delta T$ and
therefore $Q$ decrease exponentially.

**Reference:** Incropera *et al.* (2007), Ch. 3.
Instantaneous Cooling / Heating Rate

| Symbol | Description | Units |
|--------|-------------|-------|
| $Q_{\text{jacket}}$ | Heat transfer through jacket (= $U A (T_{jacket} - T)$; positive when the jacket heats the batch) | W |
| $P_{\text{agitator}}$ | Impeller power dissipation (always heats) | W |
| $Q_{\text{rxn}}$ | Reaction heat (positive = exothermic, heats) | W |
| $\rho \, V \, C_p$ | Thermal mass of batch | J/K |

The *Initial dT/dt* KPI is $\lvert U A (T_{jacket} - T_{start}) + P_{agitator}\rvert / (\rho V C_p)$ in K/min (reaction heat excluded), so agitator heat slows cooling and speeds heating.
Analytical Batch Time (Log-Mean)

items.latex: t = \frac{\rho \, V \, C_p}{U \, A} \, \ln \frac{T_{\text{start}} - T_{\text{jacket}}}{T_{\text{end}} - T_{\text{jacket}}}

items.text:
Assumes constant $U$, $A$, and jacket temperature, with no agitator heat or
reaction heat. This is the standard analytical solution for an
exponentially-decaying driving force.

**Reference:** Incropera *et al.* (2007). [*Fundamentals of Heat and Mass Transfer*](https://openlibrary.org/isbn/0471457280), Ch. 5.
Transient Model — Constant Jacket Temperature (Euler Integration)

items.latex: \frac{dT}{dt} = \frac{U \, A \,(T_{\text{jacket}} - T) + P_{\text{agitator}} + Q_{\text{rxn}}}{\rho \, V \, C_p}

items.text:
A forward Euler integration of the energy balance at each time step.

**Sign convention:**
- $U \cdot A \cdot (T_{\text{jacket}} - T)$: positive when jacket is hotter (heating), negative when cooler (cooling)
- $P_{\text{agitator}}$: always positive (adds heat to batch)
- $Q_{\text{rxn}}$: positive = exothermic (adds heat)

Integration stops when $T$ reaches $T_{\text{target}}$ or $t$ reaches $t_{\text{max}}$.
Transient Model — Variable Jacket Temperature (NTU-Effectiveness)

When the jacket fluid has a finite flow rate, the outlet temperature differs
from the inlet. The NTU-effectiveness method models this:

| Symbol | Description | Units |
|--------|-------------|-------|
| $\mathrm{NTU}$ | Number of Transfer Units | — |
| $\varepsilon$ | Heat exchanger effectiveness | — |
| $\dot{m}_j$ | Jacket mass flow rate | kg/s |
| $C_{p,j}$ | Jacket fluid specific heat capacity | J/(kg·K) |
| $T_{j,\text{in}}$ | Jacket inlet temperature (constant) | °C |
| $T_{j,\text{out}}$ | Jacket outlet temperature (varies) | °C |

At each time step, $Q_{\text{jacket}}$ is computed using the current batch
temperature and the effectiveness, then the batch temperature is updated
via the same Euler integration as the constant-jacket model.

**Key insight:** Lower jacket flow rates → higher NTU → higher effectiveness
but also higher jacket outlet temperature, which reduces the effective $\Delta T$.

**Reference:** Incropera *et al.* (2007). [*Fundamentals of Heat and Mass Transfer*](https://openlibrary.org/isbn/0471457280), Ch. 11 (Heat Exchangers).

Wetted Heat-Transfer Area

The wetted heat-transfer area is computed from the liquid height and vessel
geometry. When liquid partially fills the bottom dish, only the wetted
fraction of the dish area is counted.

| Bottom Dish Type | $h_{\text{dish}}$ | $A_{\text{dish,full}}$ |
|-----------------|-------------------|----------------------|
| Flat | 0 | $\pi/4 \cdot D_T^2$ |
| 2:1 Elliptical | $D_T / 4$ | $1.084 \cdot D_T^2$ |
| Torispherical / DIN | $0.194 \cdot D_T$ | $0.99 \cdot D_T^2$ |
| Conical (45°) | $D_T / 2$ | $\sqrt{2} \cdot \pi/4 \cdot D_T^2$ |

A measured dish depth from the vessel database replaces the default $h_{dish}$.

**Reference:** Head geometry per DIN 28011 (torispherical) and DIN 28013 (semi-ellipsoidal); oblate-spheroid and cone lateral-area formulas.
